newsitem.title: POLAND: IMF calls for more flexible zloty rate. [CORRECTED 15:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: IMF calls for more flexible zloty rate. [CORRECTED 15:45 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects headline and text throughout to make clear the IMF does not recommend scrapping the devaluation mechanism. The recommendation is only for a more flexible zloty rate).

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) called on Wednesday for the Polish zloty to be allowed more flexibility within its 14-percent trading band centre around the central bank's parity rate to curb inflation.
The zloty is currently devalued against a basket of five western currencies, in a mechanism called the crawling peg, by one percent a month to compensate for high inflation.

"While the crawling peg regime had served Poland well in the past, (IMF) directors generally considered that a more flexible exchange rate policy could increase the effectiveness of monetary policy and bring about lower inflation," it said.

"What this means is that we recommend more flexibility within the crawl -- to let the rate move somewhat more freely around the central parity," IMF's representative in Poland, Marcus Rodlauer, told Reuters.
Rodlauer made clear the IMF did not mean to recommend a scrapping of the crawling peg.
The IMF report, based on the fund's review of the Polish economy in January 1996, was scheduled for issue on Friday but prematurely released by Polish news organisations on Wednesday.

Last year the National Bank of Poland allowed the zloty to float within a 14 percent band centered around the NBP's so-called parity rate -- calculated daily against the basket of currencies and the devalution factor.
However, it has often intervened against the rising zloty at between 2.5 and three percent from the central parity rate.
All of 1995 and early in 1996 the zloty has been under strong appreciation pressure from a large current account surplus, but the pressure has eased in recent months.
Poland has set an abitious goal of lowering year-on-year inflation to 17 percent in December 1996 from 21.6 percent in December 1995 and take it down to a single digit by the year 2000.
The independent Polish central bank sees this year's inflation at just below 18 percent while many banks expect it might be at around 19 percent.
